Maximos of Gallipoli
max'i-mos
n. (d. c. 1633; translator of the New Testament into spoken Greek, printed at Geneva in 1638)
Maximos, from Latin maximus, greatest; Gallipoli, from Greek Kallipolis, the beautiful city.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Maximos Kallipolites was a monk of Gallipoli whom Cyril Lucaris commissioned to translate the New Testament out of the Greek of the original into the spoken Greek of his own day, on the ground that ordinary Greeks could no longer understand the text read in their churches. He worked at it with Antoine Leger, Geneva's chaplain at Constantinople, finished it about 1632, and died before it was printed. It came off the press at Geneva in 1638, with the original and the vernacular in parallel columns and a preface defending the whole enterprise, in the same year Lucaris was strangled. It was attacked at once as a Protestant intrusion and the later synods condemned it. The dictionary records him because the Lord's own parable makes understanding the difference between the seed that is snatched away and the seed that bears: “and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart” (Mat 13:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native, belonging to the country of one's birth; plain as evident, clear, not obscure; and to enlighten as to make clear to the understanding, to instruct.

expand to see more

VERNACULAR, a. [L. vernaculus.] Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.

PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure or difficult.

ENLIGHTEN, v.t. To make clear to the understanding; to instruct; to illuminate with knowledge.

HUNDREDFOLD, n. A hundred times as much; the increase of a hundred to one.

STATUTE, n. [L. statutum.] An act of the legislature; a law; a special law or decree.

Key Scripture

Mat 13:19 — "When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side."

Mat 13:23 — "But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty."

Pro 8:9 — "They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge."

Psa 19:8 — "The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes."

Modern Corruption

Monk of Gallipoli commissioned by Cyril Lucaris to translate the New Testament into spoken Greek; completed about 1632 and printed at Geneva in 1638, the year Lucaris died.

expand to see more

The corruption here is the argument used against the translation, which is the oldest argument there is and is still in use. It was said that the received Greek text was sacred in its form as well as its substance, that a vernacular rendering would flatten its mysteries, and that the people did not need to understand what they heard so much as to receive it reverently. The dictionary answers that an unintelligible reading is not a reverent one, and notes that the same arguments were made in Latin against the same work in the West, by men who would not have accepted them about any other book.

The principle to recover is that understanding is not an optional refinement of hearing but the thing that distinguishes fruitful hearing from the other kind. The Lord's own exposition of the sower turns on it: the wayside hearer is the one of whom it is said “and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one” (Mat 13:19). The good ground is described by the same faculty working: “he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit” (Mat 13:23). Wisdom claims to be plain to the man who will understand (Pro 8:9), and the Psalm says what the commandment does when it is received: “the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes” (Psa 19:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek suniemi (G4920), to understand or comprehend; Greek karpophoreo (G2592), to bear fruit.

expand to see more

Greek suniemi (G4920) — to put together, to understand, to comprehend; Matthew 13:19 and 13:23.

Greek harpazo (G726) — to seize, to snatch away; “catcheth away that which was sown”, Matthew 13:19.

Greek karpophoreo (G2592) — to bear fruit, to be fruitful; Matthew 13:23.

Hebrew nakoach (H5228) — straightforward, plain, right; Proverbs 8:9.

Hebrew 'or (H215) — to be light, to give light, to enlighten; Psalm 19:8.

Usage

"“and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one” (Mat 13:19) — ordinary Greeks could no longer follow the text read in church."

"“he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit” (Mat 13:23) — the New Testament in spoken Greek, printed Geneva 1638."

"“the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes” (Psa 19:8) — condemned at once as a Protestant intrusion."
